summary.text: The proof’s core is a coupling between masses \(n\) and \(n+1\): the latter evolution is the former plus one “defect” unit, whose position advances exactly when its current cell has odd mass; after the \(n\)-process stabilizes, this defect advances one cell per step until reaching the new final cell. A conserved-mass/contiguous-support invariant, applied to the penultimate configuration, forces its front and unique leftmost heavy cell to be \(n-2\) with mass \(2\), and hence places the defect at stabilization at \(n-2\) or \(n-1\), so the coupled process needs respectively two or one further steps.

full_proof.text:
We number the cells by \(0,1,2,\ldots\), from left to right. It is convenient first to express a configuration as a function
\[
 f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N,
\]
where \(f(i)\) is the mass in cell \(i\), and all but finitely many values are zero. Define the one-step evolution operator \(T\) by
\[
 (Tf)(0)=\left\lceil\frac{f(0)}2\right\rceil

a\quad\text{and}\quad
 (Tf)(i)=\left\lceil\frac{f(i)}2\right\rceil+
              \left\lfloor\frac{f(i-1)}2\right\rfloor\quad(i\geq 1).
\]
Equivalently, using integer division,
\[
 (Tf)(i)=\frac{f(i)+1}{2}+
 \begin{cases}0,&i=0,\\ f(i-1)/2,&i>0.\end{cases}
\]
Thus each cell retains the ceiling of half its mass and passes the floor of half its mass one place to the right.

For \(n\geq1\), let
\[
 I_n(i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
 \qquad
 U_n(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<n,\\0,&i\geq n.\end{cases}
\]
The latter is the stable configuration consisting of \(n\) unit cells. Write
\[
 P_n(t)=T^t I_n.
\]
We shall prove that the first time at which \(P_n(t)=U_n\) is exactly the sequence value \(a(n)\), and then compare the evolutions for \(n\) and \(n+1\).

First, this function formulation agrees with the list formulation in the definition of the sequence. If a finite list \(L\) is extended by zeros and denoted \(\widehat L(i)\), then the untrimmed list update has at index \(i\) the value
\[
 \frac{\widehat L(i)+1}{2}+
 \begin{cases}0,&i=0,\\ \widehat L(i-1)/2,&i>0,\end{cases}
\]
which is exactly \((T\widehat L)(i)\). Deleting trailing zero entries does not change the zero-extended function. Hence, by induction on the number of steps, the zero extension of the list obtained after \(t\) list updates from \([n]\) is \(P_n(t)\).

There is no ambiguity in passing back from functions to lists: every updated list has no trailing zero, as does the list of \(n\) ones, and two finite lists without trailing zeros that have the same zero extension must be equal. Consequently,
\[
 \text{the list at time }t\text{ equals }[1,\ldots,1]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_n(t)=U_n.
\]
The fold over a range used in the definition is simply repeated application of the same update, so
\[
 a(n)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N:P_n(t)=U_n\},                         \tag{1}
\]
provided this set is nonempty. We next prove that it is.

We use a basic structural property. Say that a configuration \(f\) of total mass \(n\) has structure \(S_n\) if there is a front position \(r<n\) such that
\[
 f(i)\geq1\quad(0\leq i\leq r),\qquad f(i)=0\quad(i>r),          \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{n}f(i)=n.                                          \tag{3}
\]
Initially this holds with \(r=0\). It is preserved by one update. Indeed, cells through \(r\) remain positive, since each retains the ceiling of at least half of a positive mass. No mass can appear beyond \(r+1\), and
\[
 (Tf)(r+1)=\left\lfloor\frac{f(r)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus the new front is \(r+1\) if \(f(r)\geq2\), and is \(r\) if \(f(r)=1\). Total mass is preserved. More explicitly, for every \(K\), telescoping the incoming and retained contributions gives
\[
 \sum_{i=0}^{K}(Tf)(i)+\left\lfloor\frac{f(K)}2\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{i=0}^{K}f(i).                                           \tag{4}
\]
Taking \(K=n\), where \(f(n)=0\), proves (3) for \(Tf\). Finally, the new front is still less than \(n\): if it were \(n\), the \(n+1\) positive cells from \(0\) through \(n\) would have total mass at least \(n+1\), contrary to (3). Thus every \(P_n(t)\) has structure \(S_n\).

If a configuration with structure \(S_n\) has every cell at most one, then all cells through its front equal one. Its mass is therefore the number of these cells, so (3) forces the front to be \(n-1\); hence the configuration is exactly \(U_n\). It follows that every nonterminal structured configuration has some cell of mass at least two.

To prove termination, define the tail mass to the right of \(k\) by
\[
 R_k(f)=\sum_{i=k+1}^{n}f(i),
\]
and the potential
\[
 \Phi(f)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}R_k(f).
\]
This is the total rightward displacement of all mass, counted with multiplicity. From (4), applied once at \(k\) and once at \(n\), one obtains, whenever \(f(n)=0\),
\[
 R_k(Tf)=R_k(f)+\left\lfloor\frac{f(k)}2\right\rfloor.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Phi(Tf)=\Phi(f)+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left\lfloor\frac{f(k)}2\right\rfloor.       \tag{5}
\]
If \(f\neq U_n\), some cell \(b<n\) has mass at least two, so the final sum in (5) is at least one. Thus, if the process never reached \(U_n\), its potential after \(t\) steps would be at least \(t\). On the other hand each tail has mass at most the total mass \(n\), and there are \(n\) tails, so \(\Phi\leq n^2\) at every time. Taking \(t=n^2+1\) is impossible. This proves termination and justifies (1). It also implies
\[
 P_n(a(n)+s)=U_n\quad\text{for every }s\geq0,                   \tag{6}
\]
because \(U_n\) is fixed by \(T\).

We now establish the coupling between consecutive masses. For a position \(g\), let \(e_g\) denote one unit at \(g\):
\[
 e_g(j)=\begin{cases}1,&j=g,\\0,&j\neq g.\end{cases}
\]
A direct examination of parity gives the fundamental identity
\[
 T(f+e_g)=Tf+e_{g'},
 \qquad
 g'=g+\begin{cases}1,&f(g)\text{ is odd},\\0,&f(g)\text{ is even}.
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{7}
\]
Here addition is pointwise. To see (7), cells other than \(g\) and \(g+1\) are plainly unaffected by the extra unit. If \(f(g)=2q\), then changing it to \(2q+1\) increases the retained ceiling from \(q\) to \(q+1\), while the transmitted floor remains \(q\); the extra unit stays at \(g\). If \(f(g)=2q+1\), changing it to \(2q+2\) leaves the retained ceiling equal to \(q+1\) but increases the transmitted floor from \(q\) to \(q+1\); the extra unit moves to \(g+1\). This also covers \(g=0\), with no incoming term on its left.

Define the defect position \(d_n(t)\) recursively by
\[
 d_n(0)=0,
 \qquad
 d_n(t+1)=d_n(t)+
 \begin{cases}1,&P_n(t)(d_n(t))\text{ is odd},\\0,&P_n(t)(d_n(t))\text{ is even}.
 \end{cases}                                                     \tag{8}
\]
Since \(I_{n+1}=I_n+e_0\), induction using (7) proves
\[
 P_{n+1}(t)=P_n(t)+e_{d_n(t)}                                   \tag{9}
\]
for every \(t\). Thus the sole difference between the two evolutions is a single extra unit whose position is governed by (8).

The main task is to locate this defect when the \(n\)-process first stabilizes. For \(n\geq2\), we prove the following stronger invariant at every time \(t<a(n)\). There exist positions \(r,b\) such that:

1. \(r<n\), and \(b\leq r\);
2. \(P_n(t)(i)\geq1\) for \(i\leq r\), and \(P_n(t)(i)=0\) for \(i>r\);
3. \(P_n(t)(b)\geq2\), while \(P_n(t)(i)=1\) for every \(i<b\);
4. the total mass through position \(n\) is \(n\);
5. the defect is close to the active interval in the precise sense
\[
 b\leq d_n(t)+1,
 \qquad
 d_n(t)\leq r+1.                                                \tag{10}
\]
Thus \(r\) is the front, and \(b\) is the first cell whose mass is at least two.

At time zero take \(r=b=0\). The only nonzero mass is \(n\geq2\), the defect is at zero, and all assertions hold.

We verify preservation under one step, provided the new configuration is still nonterminal. Write \(f=P_n(t)\), \(g=d_n(t)\), and let
\[
 g'=g+\begin{cases}1,&f(g)\text{ odd},\\0,&f(g)\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}
\]
As above, the new front is determined by the old front mass. If \(f(r)\geq2\), then \((Tf)(r+1)=\lfloor f(r)/2\rfloor\geq1\), so the new front is \(r'=r+1\). If \(f(r)=1\), no mass moves from \(r\) to \(r+1\), so \(r'=r\). Positivity, support, total mass, and \(r'<n\) follow exactly as in the proof of the weaker structural property. Also \(g'\leq r'+1\): the defect advances by at most one; if it was at \(r+1\) while the front does not advance, then \(f(g)=0\), which is even, so the defect itself does not advance.

We next determine the new first cell of mass at least two. Every cell strictly before \(b\) remains one: at position zero, \(\lceil1/2\rceil=1\), and at a later position the retained contribution from its own unit mass and the transmitted contribution from the preceding unit mass are \(1+0=1\).

If \(f(b)\geq3\), then \((Tf)(b)\geq2\) (including the possible incoming contribution), so we may take \(b'=b\). The bound \(b'\leq g'+1\) follows from \(b\leq g+1\) and \(g'\geq g\).

The remaining case is \(f(b)=2\). Then \((Tf)(b)=1\): its retained contribution is one, and if \(b>0\), the preceding cell is one and transmits zero. If \(b=r\), this would actually make the next configuration terminal. Indeed, cells before \(b\) become one, cell \(b\) becomes one, the new cell \(r+1\) receives \(\lfloor2/2\rfloor=1\), and every later cell is zero; all masses would then be at most one, hence by the structural property the target would have been reached. Since we are assuming the next time is nonterminal, we must have \(b<r\). Positivity gives \(f(b+1)\geq1\), and therefore
\[
 (Tf)(b+1)=\left\lceil\frac{f(b+1)}2\right\rceil+ rac{f(b)}2\geq1+1=2.
\]
So in this case take \(b'=b+1\). All earlier cells are one, including the new value at \(b\).

It remains only to check \(b+1\leq g'+1\), or \(b\leq g'\). If \(b\leq g\), this is immediate. Otherwise (10) forces \(g=b-1\). The cell at \(g\) is then one, hence odd, so the defect advances to \(g'=b\), as required. This completes the preservation proof. By induction, the strong invariant holds at every time before \(a(n)\).

We now inspect the last nonterminal configuration. Since \(n\geq2\), the initial configuration is not \(U_n\), so \(a(n)\geq1\). Write
\[
 a(n)=p+1,
 \qquad C=P_n(p).
\]
Then \(C\) satisfies the strong invariant, while
\[
 TC=P_n(a(n))=U_n.                                               \tag{11}
\]
Let \(r,b\) be its front and first mass-at-least-two position.

First we show
\[
 r=n-2.                                                         \tag{12}
\]
Because \((TC)(n-1)=U_n(n-1)=1\), support propagation implies \(r\geq n-2\): if \(r<n-2\), then even after one step no mass could reach position \(n-1\). On the other hand \(r<n\), so the only alternative to \(r\leq n-2\) is \(r=n-1\). But in that case all \(n\) cells from \(0\) through \(n-1\) have mass at least one, and the cell \(b\) has mass at least two. Their total mass would therefore be at least \(n+1\), contradicting the total mass \(n\). Hence (12) holds.

Next,
\[
 C(b)=2.                                                        \tag{13}
\]
If instead \(C(b)\geq3\), then its retained half alone is at least two, so \((TC)(b)\geq2\), contrary to (11), since every occupied cell of \(U_n\) has mass one.

Furthermore,
\[
 b=r.                                                           \tag{14}
\]
For if \(b<r\), then \(C(b+1)\geq1\), and by (13)
\[
 (TC)(b+1)=\left\lceil\frac{C(b+1)}2\right\rceil+ rac{C(b)}2
 \geq1+1=2,
\]
again contradicting (11). Thus the last nonterminal configuration has its first mass-two cell exactly at its front \(r=n-2\), that cell has mass exactly two, all earlier cells have mass one, and all later cells have mass zero.

Let \(g=d_n(p)\). The defect bounds (10), together with \(b=r\), say
\[
 r\leq g+1,
 \qquad g\leq r+1.                                              \tag{15}
\]
We compute its position one step later, namely \(d_n(a(n))\), by splitting into all possibilities relative to \(r\).

If \(g<r\), then (15) forces \(g=r-1\). Since all cells before \(r\) have mass one, \(C(g)=1\) is odd, so the defect advances one place. Hence
\[
 d_n(a(n))=g+1=r=n-2.
\]
If \(g=r\), then \(C(g)=C(r)=2\) is even, so the defect stays at \(r=n-2\).
If \(g>r\), then (15) forces \(g=r+1\). This is beyond the front, so \(C(g)=0\), which is even, and the defect stays at
\[
 r+1=n-1.
\]
We have therefore proved the crucial dichotomy
\[
 d_n(a(n))=n-2\quad\text{or}\quad d_n(a(n))=n-1                 \tag{16}
\]
for every \(n\geq2\).

It remains to translate the defect position into the stabilization time for mass \(n+1\). First observe that
\[
 U_{n+1}=U_n+e_n.                                                \tag{17}
\]
Combining (9) and (17), we claim that for every \(t\),
\[
 P_{n+1}(t)=U_{n+1}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 P_n(t)=U_n\ \text{ and }\ d_n(t)=n.                            \tag{18}
\]
The reverse implication is immediate. For the forward implication, compare both sides at position \(n\). Every \(P_n(t)\) is supported strictly before \(n\), so \(P_n(t)(n)=0\), and \(U_n(n)=0\). The right side of (17) has one unit at \(n\); therefore (9) can equal it only if the defect is at \(n\). Once the defect positions agree, cancelling the identical added unit pointwise gives \(P_n(t)=U_n\).

After time \(a(n)\), equation (6) says that the background configuration remains \(U_n\). At every position below \(n\), \(U_n\) has value one, which is odd, while at position \(n\) it has value zero, which is even. Consequently, once the background has stabilized, the defect moves right by one at every step until it reaches \(n\), and then stays there. If
\[
 d=d_n(a(n))\leq n,
\]
then explicitly
\[
 d_n(a(n)+s)=\min(d+s,n).                                       \tag{19}
\]
This follows immediately by induction from the defect recursion (8).

Equations (18) and (19), together with the minimality of \(a(n)\), now give
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+(n-d_n(a(n))).                                     \tag{20}
\]
Indeed, at the time on the right, the \(n\)-background is stable and the defect has just reached \(n\), so (18) shows that the \((n+1)\)-process is stable. No earlier time can work: before \(a(n)\), the \(n\)-background is not yet \(U_n\); from time \(a(n)\) onward but before the displayed time, (19) says the defect has not yet reached \(n\). These are precisely the two necessary conditions in (18).

For \(n\geq2\), substitute (16) into (20). If \(d_n(a(n))=n-1\), then
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+1;
\]
if \(d_n(a(n))=n-2\), then
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]

Finally consider \(n=1\). The initial mass-one configuration is already stable, so \(a(1)=0\), and its defect starts at \(d_1(0)=0\). Formula (20), whose coupling and minimality argument also applies here, gives
\[
 a(2)=a(1)+(1-0)=a(1)+1.
\]
Thus for every integer \(n\geq1\),
\[
 a(n+1)=a(n)+1\quad\text{or}\quad a(n+1)=a(n)+2.
\]
Equivalently, every finite difference \(a(n+1)-a(n)\) is either \(1\) or \(2\), as claimed.
